archetype.name: Lottery Team (run-first, pass game broken)
archetype.definition: A club out of real contention whose run game and special teams keep games close for a while, but whose passing offense is the worst in the league and whose turnovers decide most Sundays.

report.headline: Taylor's run game is real; the passing game and turnovers are sinking everything
report.take:
The Colts are a 3-7 team that is roughly as bad as its record says, maybe a shade unlucky. Their point differential implies 4.8 wins, and the wins-over-expected mark of -1.79 says a couple of close games went the wrong way. The efficiency numbers don't argue for a hidden contender, though. Net EPA ranks 29th, the offense 31st, and points allowed 30th. This is a team losing on both sides of the ball, with one dominant cause.

That cause is the passing game. Daniel Jones has started all ten games, and the offense's pass EPA of -0.175 ranks dead last. Pass EPA was negative in nine of ten games, with Kansas City the only exception. The bottoms show how bad it gets: -17.6 at Jacksonville, and -11.2 in the win over Miami, when Jones threw for 108 yards and the Colts survived on 172 rushing yards. The run game is the healthy part. Rush EPA ranks 7th, run success 7th, and Jonathan Taylor carries a heavy load, which is why the Colts rank 8th in time of possession and lean run (pass rate over expected -2.9). The turnovers are what turn a bad offense into a losing one: 19 giveaways against 7 takeaways, a -12 differential, with multiple giveaways in eight of ten games.

The defense is better on a per-play basis than the points suggest, but it is built in a way that bleeds. The Colts get off the field on third down (5th) and rank 13th in success rate allowed. They also allow the 31st-ranked explosive pass rate, generate little pressure (27th), and have forced only 6 takeaways by the season count (31st). Many of the 27.7 points a game allowed come from chunk plays and from short fields the offense hands over. Against the run they are leaky by EPA (29th), and lead backs have feasted, scoring 4.7 PPR points a game over their averages, the worst mark in the league.

History makes this look like 2022 more than a slow fade. Last year's offense ranked 7th in EPA. In 2022 it collapsed to 31st with a league-worst turnover margin, which is exactly the shape of this season. A pass offense this bad rarely flips midseason with the same quarterback. Now both starting tackles are banged up, so the more likely path is more of the same: competitive when Taylor controls the clock and the ball stays secure, blown out when it doesn't.

strengths.title: Taylor-led run game stays efficient
strengths.body: The rushing attack is genuinely above average. It ranks 7th in run EPA and run success, with a middle-of-the-pack line in yards before contact, so it isn't purely a product of game script. It is the one phase that travels week to week, and the reason the Colts can win ugly, as they did against Miami. Losing both starting tackles threatens it more than anything opponents have done.

strengths.title: Third-down defense ends drives
strengths.body: The defense allows conversions at a 5th-best rate, and its overall success rate allowed ranks 13th, so it wins plenty of individual snaps. That keeps games shorter and helps the ball-control plan. It is sustainable as long as the secondary is healthy, which it may not be this week.

strengths.title: Special teams and discipline
strengths.body: Special teams add 1.61 EPA a game (6th), and the team ranks 3rd in fewest penalties per game. These are small edges, but for an offense that can't sustain drives through the air, hidden yardage matters. The penalty cleanliness has slipped lately; Miami cost 83 yards.

concerns.title: League-worst passing offense
concerns.body: Pass EPA ranks 32nd, the line ranks 28th in QB hit rate allowed, and Jones has produced negative pass EPA in nine of ten starts. This isn't one bad stretch; it is the baseline. With both starting tackles hurt, protection is more likely to get worse than better.

concerns.title: Turnover margin swallowing games
concerns.body: Nineteen giveaways against seven takeaways is a -12 margin, 31st per game. Part of the takeaway side is variance that should drift up some. The giveaway side, though, tracks with a pressured, inefficient passer and is less likely to fix itself. It also explains why a defense with decent per-play numbers allows 27-plus points a game.

concerns.title: No pass rush, explosives allowed
concerns.body: The defense ranks 27th in pressure rate and 31st in explosive pass rate allowed. Quarterbacks get time, and when the coverage breaks it breaks for big gains. That is a structural flaw rather than bad luck, and it is magnified with both starting corners questionable.

trend.note: A 2-2 start built on a run-heavy road win at Washington gave way to a losing run through October, including a 42-7 loss at Jacksonville. The Miami win came with 108 passing yards and -11.2 pass EPA, so it doesn't signal a turnaround.

nextGame.headline: Short week, banged-up tackles, against the league's sack leaders
nextGame.body:
The Colts go to Houston on four days' rest as 11.5-point underdogs (+470) in a rematch of their 19-17 Week 3 win. They won that game despite three turnovers and four sacks allowed. Houston is 3-6 but much better than that by efficiency: net EPA ranks 13th, the passing offense 7th, and its wins over expected (-1.82) is as unlucky as Indianapolis's. The matchup is lopsided where it hurts most. Houston's defense leads the league in sacks and ranks 2nd in sack rate, facing the league's worst passing offense. Houston's own weakness is the run game, 25th in run EPA and 29th in run success, which happens to be the one thing the Colts' defense handles worst.

Availability swings this heavily. Starting tackle Jalen Travis is out, and Bernhard Raimann is questionable after entering the concussion protocol, which is hard to clear on a Thursday turnaround. Both starting corners, Charvarius Ward and Sauce Gardner, are questionable. Linebacker Akeem Davis-Gaither is on IR and Jaylon Carlies is out. Houston is short too: edge rusher Danielle Hunter and linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair are out, receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. is out, and lead back Woody Marks is doubtful. Hunter's absence softens the rush a little, but Houston's sack numbers suggest the pressure doesn't depend on one player.

waysToWin.title: Ride Taylor and shorten the game
waysToWin.body: The Colts' run game ranks 7th in EPA. Houston's run defense is middling at 21st by play-by-play EPA and is missing Al-Shaair in the middle. Long drives keep Jones out of obvious passing downs against the league's best sack defense and keep Stroud on the sideline. It is the same formula that beat Miami.

waysToWin.title: Houston can't run without Marks
waysToWin.body: Houston's run game is 25th in run EPA with 3.32 yards a carry, and its lead back is doubtful. That shields the Colts' worst defensive weakness, lead backs, and makes Houston one-dimensional. A one-dimensional offense is easier for a defense that ranks 5th on third down.

waysToWin.title: Target the WR2 and take shots
waysToWin.body: Houston has been soft against second receivers (+4.0 PPR over average, 30th) and ranks 24th in deep-pass EPA allowed. It is stingy with tight ends, so the passing plan should run through Downs and Allen rather than Warren. If Jones gets clean looks off play-action, a few chunk gains are there.

waysToLose.title: Backup tackles versus the sack leaders
waysToLose.body: Houston leads the league in sacks and ranks 2nd in sack rate. The Colts' line was already 28th in QB hit rate allowed with its starters, and now Travis is out and Raimann is in protocol. Drive-killing sacks and strip-sacks are the most direct path to a blowout.

waysToLose.title: Stroud hits a thin secondary
waysToLose.body: Houston's passing offense ranks 7th in EPA. The Colts already allow the 31st-ranked explosive pass rate with a weak pass rush, and both starting corners could sit. Even without Harrison Jr., a few explosive completions could put the Colts in a hole their passing game can't climb out of.

waysToLose.title: Turnovers flip the field again
waysToLose.body: The Colts gave the ball away three times in the first meeting and escaped. Their -12 turnover margin says that won't keep happening, and short fields against a top-10 scoring offense turn a close game into the double-digit loss the line expects.

nextGame.watch: Who lines up at the two tackle spots, and how often Jones is hit on early downs. If Taylor's runs keep the Colts out of third-and-long, this stays close; if not, Houston's pass rush ends it early.

restOfSeason.body:
The schedule after Houston is split. Philadelphia (2-7) and Tennessee (1-8) on the road are winnable, and the Giants at home are a coin flip. Cincinnati, Cleveland and Jacksonville are tougher, and Jacksonville has already beaten the Colts 42-7. Some of the record is bad luck in close games and on takeaways, so the defense should force a few more turnovers and the margins should even out slightly. The core problem, a last-ranked passing offense, is not a luck issue and is unlikely to improve with injuries piling up on the line.

Expect a team that wins when Taylor controls the clock against weak opponents and loses comfortably to good ones. The run game and special teams should hold up. Points allowed may drop a bit if the giveaways ease, but the explosive-play leak in the secondary keeps a floor under them. A finish around five wins is the realistic center.
swingFactors: Ward and Gardner returning at corner

confidence.note: Ten games with a stable QB and a consistent passing collapse, but heavy injury uncertainty.
